title: The gate runner is a single Node entry point; one illustrative GitHub Actions workflow is shipped; alternate providers wire the same script
context: A blueprint that ships CI configuration has two shapes to pick between. Shape one: contribute a provider-specific configuration file (a GitHub Actions workflow YAML, a GitLab CI YAML, a CircleCI config) with every gate spelled in that provider's runner language. Shape two: contribute a Node entry-point script that any provider invokes with one command line, and ship one illustrative provider example as a starting point. Shape one locks the project to the picked provider; shape two lets any provider that can run Node host the pipeline. The rcf-lite tier does not privilege one provider.
decision: The blueprint ships shape two. The gate runner is a single Node entry-point script the project realises under its source tree; every gate-specific piece of logic (spawning the child, capturing streams, writing per-gate reports, writing the aggregate report, surfacing failure) lives in Node. The blueprint's package resources include exactly one illustrative provider workflow: `assets/ci-provider-examples/github-actions.yml`, chosen because GitHub Actions is the most widely deployed among rcf-lite candidate projects. The guide names GitLab CI, CircleCI, Buildkite, and Jenkins as equally supported and describes the four-point mapping (job trigger event, Node setup, single-line entry-point invocation, artefact upload) for each. No provider-specific configuration file for those runners is shipped at v1.0.0. A future blueprint that ships one, or a project that hand-authors one, wires the same Node entry point.
consequences: A project on any CI provider that can run Node (every mainstream provider) hosts the pipeline with a one-line invocation. Moving between providers is a rewrite of the trigger definition and the artefact-upload step, not a rewrite of the gates. The illustrative GitHub Actions workflow is a starting point, not a blessed choice: an operator moving to another provider translates the four mapping points and keeps the entry-point invocation unchanged. The blueprint does not carry the maintenance cost of a matrix of provider examples; each example would need to track that provider's syntax changes and version pins, which is a per-provider decision the project owns.

alternativesConsidered.name: Ship a matrix of provider-specific configuration files (GHA + GitLab CI + CircleCI + Buildkite + Jenkins) at v1.0.0
alternativesConsidered.summary: The blueprint contributes one configuration file per supported provider so the operator can copy the one that matches.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Every provider file needs its own version pins, its own action or plugin references, and its own syntax bumps. Five files stale at different rates and the blueprint's ship gate would include verifying every one still works on every provider. One worked example plus the mapping paragraph is the sharper contribution.

alternativesConsidered.name: Ship a bash gate runner instead of Node
alternativesConsidered.summary: The gate runner is a shell script the CI provider invokes.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Bash is not portable across the operator's development host (macOS default bash is 3.2, Windows has no bash without WSL, and cross-platform bash gymnastics are the shape that ships broken). Node runs identically on every host that ships an rcf-lite project, and the same Node runtime that runs the underlying rcf CLI runs the gate runner without a second toolchain.
